keyVerseText: And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other . with: or, with a trumpet, and a great voice
rootMeaning: The word ἄκρον (ákron) is the neuter form of an adjective likely related to the base of ἀκμή (akmḗn), which conveys the idea of a highest or extreme point. The root ἀκμή itself means 'yet' or 'just now,' suggesting a notion of immediacy or being at the very edge. This etymological background enriches the understanding of ἄκρον as not merely a physical extremity but as a critical point of culmination or the utmost boundary, going beyond the simple English gloss of 'tip' or 'end.'
usageInScripture: In Scripture, ἄκρον appears six times, consistently conveying the idea of an extremity or utmost part, whether physical like a mountain peak or metaphorical as the highest pitch or degree. The top translations include 'one end,' 'the uttermost part,' 'the tip,' and 'the top,' showing a range that highlights both tangible edges and figurative heights. This consistency in usage underscores ἄκρον as a term denoting the furthest or most elevated point in various contexts, emphasizing boundaries and limits.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἄκρον as the utmost extremity or highest point deepens our appreciation of biblical descriptions that speak of God's sovereignty over all creation, from the highest mountain to the farthest horizon. This word reminds believers that God's power and presence extend to every 'end' and 'height,' leaving nothing outside His domain. Theologically, it points to the comprehensive scope of divine authority and the fulfillment of His promises, which reach to the very edges of heaven and earth. Recognizing this helps Christians trust in God's control over all things, even those that seem distant or out of reach.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 24:31 states, 'And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.' Here, ἄκρον signifies the complete extent of heaven, emphasizing the totality of God's gathering work. The use of ἄκρον highlights that no part of the heavens is excluded, reinforcing the promise that Christ's elect will be gathered from every extremity, underscoring the all-encompassing nature of God's redemptive plan.
